title: Metals and Their Properties
description: Metallic bonding, reactivity series, and why metals behave the way they do

concepts.title: The Metallic Bond Revisited
concepts.contentHtml:
About 80% of elements are metals. Their characteristic properties — lustrous, ductile, malleable, thermally and electrically conductive — all stem from metallic bonding: positive metal ions embedded in a delocalised sea of electrons.

This electron sea is responsible for:
— Conductivity: free electrons carry charge and thermal energy
— Malleability: layers of ions can slide without breaking the bond
— Lustre: free electrons absorb and re-emit light across all visible wavelengths

Metallic bond strength depends on the number of electrons contributed per atom and the charge density of the ion. Tungsten (melting point 3,422°C) forms an extraordinarily strong metallic lattice; mercury is liquid at room temperature because its d¹⁰ shell weakens interatomic interactions.

concepts.title: The Reactivity Series
concepts.contentHtml:
Metals differ enormously in how readily they lose electrons (oxidise). The reactivity series ranks metals from most to least reactive:

K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Ni > Sn > Pb > H > Cu > Ag > Pt > Au

Metals above hydrogen displace H₂ from dilute acids. Those above copper displace copper from copper-salt solutions. The series predicts whether a displacement reaction will occur — a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from solution.

The series also explains everyday observations: gold and platinum resist corrosion; iron rusts; sodium ignites on contact with water. The underlying measure is standard electrode potential, which we measure in electrochemistry.

concepts.title: Oxides, Hydroxides, and Acid/Base Character
concepts.contentHtml:
Metal oxides and hydroxides show characteristic acid–base behaviour:

Metal oxides are typically basic: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂; MgO + 2 HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O.
Non-metal oxides are typically acidic: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃; SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄.

Amphoteric oxides react with both acids and bases. Aluminium oxide is the classic example: Al₂O₃ + 6 HCl → 2 AlCl₃ + 3 H₂O (acts as base); Al₂O₃ + 2 NaOH + 3 H₂O → 2 Na[Al(OH)₄] (acts as acid).

This amphoteric behaviour is characteristic of metals near the metalloid borderline (Al, Zn, Sn, Pb).

title: Coordination Chemistry
description: Ligands, complex ions, and the structure of transition metal complexes

concepts.title: Complex Ions and Coordination Number
concepts.contentHtml:
A complex ion (coordination compound) consists of a central metal ion surrounded by ligands — molecules or ions that donate a lone pair to the metal, forming a coordinate (dative) bond.

The coordination number is the total number of donor atoms bonded to the central metal. Common coordination numbers:

— 2: linear, e.g., [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺
— 4: tetrahedral (e.g., [CoCl₄]²⁻) or square planar (e.g., [Pt(NH₃)₄]²⁺)
— 6: octahedral, e.g., [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺, [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺

The charge of the complex equals (metal oxidation state) + (total ligand charge). In [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻, each CN⁻ is −1 × 6 = −6, so Fe must be +2 to give overall −4.

concepts.title: Types of Ligands
concepts.contentHtml:
Ligands are classified by the number of donor atoms they offer to the metal:

— Monodentate: one donor atom. Examples: H₂O, NH₃, Cl⁻, CN⁻.
— Bidentate: two donor atoms. Examples: ethylenediamine (en), oxalate (ox²⁻).
— Polydentate (chelating): many donor atoms. EDTA⁴⁻ has 6 donor sites and wraps around one metal ion completely.

Chelating ligands form much more stable complexes than monodentate equivalents — the chelate effect. The entropic advantage of releasing multiple water molecules when a chelate displaces them drives this stability. EDTA is used in medicine (chelation therapy for heavy-metal poisoning), food preservation, and analytical chemistry.

concepts.title: Isomerism in Coordination Compounds
concepts.contentHtml:
Coordination compounds can exhibit several types of isomerism:

Geometric isomerism: in square planar or octahedral complexes, ligands can be on the same side (cis) or opposite sides (trans). Cisplatin [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] is the famous anticancer drug — its trans isomer is inactive.

Optical isomerism: tris-chelate octahedral complexes like [Co(en)₃]³⁺ are chiral (Δ and Λ isomers).

Linkage isomerism: some ligands can bind through different atoms. Nitrite (NO₂⁻) binds via N (nitro) or O (nitrito).

Isomerism in coordination compounds is not just academic — the biological activity of many metal-containing drugs depends critically on geometry.

title: Crystal Field Theory
description: d-orbital splitting, colour, and magnetic properties of transition metal complexes

concepts.title: d-Orbital Splitting
concepts.contentHtml:
In an isolated transition metal ion, all five d orbitals are degenerate (equal energy). When ligands approach along the coordination axes, their electron clouds repel certain d orbitals more than others — this is crystal field splitting.

In an octahedral field, the five d orbitals split into two groups:
— e_g (d_z² and d_x²-y²): point directly at ligands — raised in energy by +0.6Δ_o
— t_2g (d_xy, d_xz, d_yz): point between ligands — lowered by −0.4Δ_o

The splitting energy Δ_o (or 10Dq) depends on the ligand (the spectrochemical series) and the metal. Strong-field ligands like CN⁻ give large Δ_o; weak-field ligands like halides give small Δ_o.

concepts.title: Colour and Electronic Transitions
concepts.contentHtml:
Transition metal complexes are often brilliantly coloured because electrons can be promoted from lower to higher d-orbital levels by absorbing visible light. The colour observed is the complement of the absorbed colour.

Examples:
— [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺: absorbs green/yellow light → appears purple
— [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺: absorbs red light → appears blue
— [Cr(NH₃)₆]³⁺: absorbs UV/violet → appears yellow

The spectrochemical series predicts colour shifts: replacing water with stronger-field ligands increases Δ_o, shifting absorption to higher energy (shorter wavelength) and changing the colour. The energy of the d–d transition corresponds directly to Δ_o and can be measured by UV/Vis spectroscopy.

concepts.title: High-Spin vs Low-Spin and Crystal Field Stabilisation Energy
concepts.contentHtml:
For d⁴–d⁷ configurations, electrons can either be distributed across all d orbitals (high-spin, weak field) or paired preferentially in the t_2g level (low-spin, strong field). The outcome depends on whether Δ_o exceeds the electron pairing energy.

Crystal Field Stabilisation Energy (CFSE) is the extra stability gained from d-orbital splitting. It is calculated as: (electrons in t_2g × −0.4 + electrons in e_g × +0.6) × Δ_o.

High-spin complexes have more unpaired electrons → paramagnetic (attracted to magnets). Low-spin → fewer unpaired electrons; diamagnetic only if none remain (e.g. low-spin d⁶). Fe²⁺ in haemoglobin is high-spin when deoxygenated and low-spin when O₂ binds — this spin change is central to oxygen transport.

title: Solid-State Chemistry
description: Crystal structures, ionic radii, and semiconductor materials

concepts.title: Crystal Lattice Structures
concepts.contentHtml:
Ionic compounds form three-dimensional crystal lattices — repeating unit cells that pack ions to maximise attraction and minimise repulsion. The structure adopted depends mainly on the ratio of ionic radii (r⁺/r⁻).

Common structures:
— Rock salt (NaCl): 6:6 coordination, r⁺/r⁻ ≈ 0.41–0.73
— Caesium chloride (CsCl): 8:8 coordination, r⁺/r⁻ > 0.73
— Zinc blende (ZnS): 4:4 tetrahedral coordination, r⁺/r⁻ ≈ 0.22–0.41
— Fluorite (CaF₂): Ca²⁺ 8-coordinate, F⁻ 4-coordinate

The unit cell is the smallest repeating unit. For NaCl, a face-centred cubic arrangement of Cl⁻ with Na⁺ filling octahedral holes gives the familiar 1:1 stoichiometry.

concepts.title: Lattice Enthalpy and the Born–Haber Cycle
concepts.contentHtml:
Lattice enthalpy (ΔH_latt) is the energy released when gaseous ions come together to form one mole of ionic crystal. It is large and negative (exothermic) for compounds with small, highly charged ions — because the electrostatic attraction E ∝ q₁q₂/r is large.

The Born–Haber cycle is a thermochemical cycle using Hess's Law to calculate lattice enthalpy indirectly (it cannot be measured directly). Components: atomisation enthalpy, ionisation energy, electron affinity, enthalpy of formation, and lattice enthalpy. Knowing five lets you calculate the sixth.

Example: NaCl has a lattice enthalpy of about −787 kJ/mol. MgO (~−3,791 kJ/mol) is far larger because Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry double charges and are smaller.

concepts.title: Semiconductors and Band Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
Band theory extends molecular orbital ideas to solids. Atomic orbitals from millions of atoms combine to form continuous bands of allowed energy levels.

— Metals: conduction band partially filled (or valence and conduction bands overlap) — electrons flow freely.
— Insulators: large band gap (>5 eV); electrons cannot thermally jump from valence to conduction band.
— Semiconductors: small band gap (~1 eV). Silicon (1.1 eV), germanium (0.67 eV).

Doping introduces impurities to control conductivity. n-type: phosphorus (5 valence electrons) in Si adds extra electrons. p-type: boron (3 valence electrons) creates 'holes' (positive charge carriers). p–n junctions are the basis of all transistors, LEDs, and solar cells.

title: Industrial Inorganic Chemistry
description: Haber process, catalysis, and the chemistry behind everyday materials

concepts.title: The Haber Process
concepts.contentHtml:
The Haber process synthesises ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen: N₂ + 3 H₂ ⇌ 2 NH₃ (ΔH = −92 kJ/mol).

This reaction is central to global food production — ammonia is the starting material for nitrogen fertilisers. Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch developed it in the early 20th century; it now feeds roughly half the world's population.

Conditions (compromise between yield and rate):
— Temperature: ~450°C (low T favours yield by Le Chatelier, but too slow; 450°C is a compromise)
— Pressure: ~200 atm (high P favours the product side — 4 mol gas → 2 mol gas)
— Catalyst: finely divided iron with promoters (Al₂O₃, K₂O)

This is a masterclass in applying thermodynamics and kinetics together.

concepts.title: Heterogeneous Catalysis
concepts.contentHtml:
A heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase from the reactants — typically a solid catalyst with gaseous or liquid reactants. Reactions occur on the catalyst surface.

Mechanism for catalytic hydrogenation (e.g., Pd/Pt catalysts):
1. Adsorption: reactant molecules bind to surface active sites
2. Surface reaction: bonds break and form on the surface
3. Desorption: products leave the surface

Key examples:
— Iron catalyst in Haber process
— Platinum/rhodium in catalytic converters (oxidise CO, reduce NOₓ)
— Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) in Contact process (H₂SO₄ manufacture)
— Zeolites in petroleum cracking

Catalytic activity is maximised by maximising surface area — hence nanoparticle catalysts.

concepts.title: Transition Metals as Catalysts and Bioinorganic Chemistry
concepts.contentHtml:
Transition metals are prized catalysts because they have multiple stable oxidation states and can bind and release substrates readily. Key industrial examples: Fe (Haber), V₂O₅ (Contact), Ni (hydrogenation of vegetable oils), Rh/Ir (Monsanto/Cativa acetic acid process).

In biology, metal-containing enzymes run the same chemistry. Key biological examples:
— Haemoglobin: Fe²⁺ in haem binds O₂
— Nitrogenase: FeMo cofactor reduces N₂ to NH₃ at ambient temperature (compare with Haber's 450°C!)
— Cytochrome P450: Fe porphyrin oxidises drugs and xenobiotics
— Carbonic anhydrase: Zn²⁺ catalyses CO₂ ⇌ HCO₃⁻, vital for blood pH regulation

concepts.title: Why Metals Are Essential to Life
concepts.contentHtml:
About a third of all proteins use metal ions for function. Iron carries oxygen in hemoglobin. Magnesium centers chlorophyll. Zinc structures hundreds of transcription factors. Copper, manganese, molybdenum — all biologically essential at trace levels.

Metals provide chemistry organic atoms can't: redox flexibility, Lewis acidity, multi-electron transformations. Life uses them where carbon-based chemistry runs out.

concepts.title: Metalloproteins and Cofactors
concepts.contentHtml:
Metals usually sit in protein active sites coordinated to His, Cys, Asp, or Glu side chains, or in organic cofactors like heme (Fe in a porphyrin) and B12 (Co in a corrin).

Hemoglobin, myoglobin, cytochromes — all heme-iron proteins, but with different coordination geometries giving different functions (O₂ transport, electron transfer, oxidation catalysis).

Photosynthesis's water-splitting Mn₄CaO₅ cluster oxidizes water to O₂ — chemistry no synthetic catalyst has matched in performance.

concepts.title: Toxic and Therapeutic Metals
concepts.contentHtml:
Some metals are poisons. Lead and mercury substitute for essential metals (Zn, Ca) in active sites and disrupt them. Cadmium and arsenic accumulate. Chronic exposure causes neurological and developmental disease.

Other metal complexes are drugs. Cisplatin (cis-PtCl₂(NH₃)₂) cross-links DNA in cancer cells — a billion-dollar oncology drug since the 1970s. Gadolinium chelates are MRI contrast agents. Lithium salts treat bipolar disorder.

Bioinorganic chemistry sits at chemistry, biology, medicine, and toxicology. It explains why metals matter so much.

concepts.title: Metal-Carbon Bonds
concepts.contentHtml:
Organometallic compounds have direct C-M bonds. Grignard reagents (RMgX) and organolithiums (RLi) are the workhorses of nucleophilic alkylation. Transition metal complexes (Fe(CO)₅, Cp₂Fe ferrocene) opened up modern catalysis.

The discovery of ferrocene (1951) — a sandwich complex of iron between two cyclopentadienyl rings — earned Wilkinson and Fischer the 1973 Nobel and launched organometallic chemistry as a field.

concepts.title: Cross-Coupling
concepts.contentHtml:
Pd-catalyzed cross-coupling reactions form C-C bonds between two halves of a molecule. The Heck, Suzuki, Negishi, and Stille reactions all do this with different organometallic partners.

Heck, Suzuki, and Negishi shared the 2010 Nobel for this. Cross-coupling now appears in the synthesis of a large share of the drugs, agrochemicals, and electronic materials made in the past two decades.

Modern variants extend to C-N (Buchwald-Hartwig amination), C-O bonds, and C-H activation — directly functionalizing C-H bonds without prefunctionalization. The toolbox keeps growing.

concepts.title: Olefin Metathesis
concepts.contentHtml:
Metathesis: two olefins exchange their =CH-X partners. Like a square dance for double bonds. Ru-based Grubbs catalysts and Mo-based Schrock catalysts made it practical.

Chauvin, Grubbs, and Schrock shared the 2005 Nobel. Ring-closing metathesis builds rings; ring-opening polymerization (ROMP) makes new polymers.

Metathesis appeared in dozens of total syntheses (incl. drug candidates) and in industrial polymer processes. A textbook example of how organometallic catalysis transforms what's synthetically possible.

title: Catalytic Cycles
description: How a transition metal does the work

concepts.title: Elementary Steps
concepts.contentHtml:
Transition-metal catalysis proceeds through a small set of repeated elementary steps:

• Oxidative addition: a substrate's bond breaks, both pieces bind to the metal — metal's oxidation state increases by 2.
• Migratory insertion: a ligand inserts into a metal-alkyl bond.
• β-hydride elimination: an alkyl ligand decomposes back to alkene plus M-H.
• Reductive elimination: two ligands couple, leaving the metal — oxidation state decreases by 2.

Most cycles use 3-4 of these steps repeated.

concepts.title: The Suzuki Cycle in Detail
concepts.contentHtml:
Suzuki coupling: ArX + Ar'B(OH)₂ + Pd cat. → Ar-Ar' + halide + boronate.

Cycle: (1) Oxidative addition of ArX to Pd(0) → ArPdX. (2) Transmetalation with arylboronate → ArPdAr'. (3) Reductive elimination of Ar-Ar' → free product + Pd(0). (4) Repeat.

Tracking electrons through the cycle, Pd cycles between 0 and +2. Each ligand exchange is an elementary step in the broader sense.

concepts.title: Designing Catalysts
concepts.contentHtml:
The right ligands tune everything: rate, selectivity, scope. Bulky phosphines (PtBu₃, BrettPhos) accelerate sluggish steps; chiral ligands (BINAP) deliver enantioselectivity; biaryl phosphines extend the substrate scope.

The mechanism dictates the design. Slow oxidative addition? Use more electron-rich phosphine. Slow reductive elimination? Bulkier ligand. Modern catalyst design is a feedback loop between mechanistic understanding and ligand optimization.

Computational chemistry (DFT) has become a routine tool — predict transition-state energies before synthesizing the ligand.
